title: ZoomDiff: A High-Fidelity Diffusion Model for Dual-Camera Smooth Zooming

paper.title: ZoomDiff: A High-Fidelity Diffusion Model for Dual-Camera Smooth Zooming
paper.abstract:
Abstract Digital zoom transitions between dual cameras often exhibit conspicuous discontinuities in geometric structure and chromatic consistency, degrading the user experience.
While recent dual-camera smooth zoom (DCSZ) methods attempt to mitigate this by fine-tuning frame interpolation (FI) models on DCSZ data, they struggle with the large cross-view disparities and complex geometric transformations.
Considering that the generative prior of diffusion models is suitable for addressing this problem, we explore their application to DCSZ.
However, naively applying existing diffusion-based FI models still yields low-fidelity transitions due to insufficient conditional guidance, high-frequency information loss during VAE encoding, as well as inadequate temporal consistency.
To address this, we propose ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion model that leverages dual-camera inputs in both latent and pixel spaces for photo-realistic transitions.
Specifically, we first strengthen dual-image conditional guidance during the multi-step denoising process to improve geometric consistency.
Then we inject flow-aligned multi-scale features from the VAE encoder into the VAE decoder to recover high-frequency details, where flow-guided temporal consistency supervision are introduced to produce more smooth transitions.
Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that ZoomDiff outperforms state-of-the-art methods quantitatively and qualitatively.
Project page: https://jiayi-hit.github.io/ZoomDiff.github.io/ .

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Illustration of high-frequency loss in the VAE latent space. Images reconstructed from VAE latents contain less details than the original ones as indicated by yellows boxes. Modern phones are equipped with multiple fixed-focal-length cameras for digital zoom. Taking the dual-camera system as an example, it consists of a wide-angle (W) lens for primary imaging and an ultra-wide-angle (UW) lens for an even wider view. Due to the distinct deployment locations and internal characteristics ( Zhang et al. 2022 ; Lee et al. 2022 ; Alzayer et al. 2023 ; Abdelhamed et al. 2021 ) of the two cameras, a notable preview jump in geometric content and image color occurs when zooming between them, which significantly affects the user experience as they generally prefer a fluid preview. To explore the issue, ( Wu et al. 2024 ) first formulated that task as dual-camera smooth zoom (DCSZ), and tackled it from a data-centric perspective. They proposed a data construction pipeline based on 3DGS ( Kerbl et al. 2023 ) , which generates synthetic DCSZ data to fine-tune a frame interpolation (FI) model for smooth transitions. However, the results generally suffer from noticeable visual artifacts, which severely undermine the perceptual quality and zooming consistency. We argue that the main cause lies in the inherent model-task mismatch. Specifically, mainstream optical-flow-based ( Li et al. 2023 ; Cheng and Chen 2021 ; Kong et al. 2022 ; Huang et al. 2022 ; Jin et al. 2023 ) or diffusion-based ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Feng et al. 2024 ; Wan et al. 2025 ) FI models are designed for videos with smaller camera or object motion, which cannot adapt to the large cross-view disparity and complex geometric transformations between dual cameras. In other words, a task-specific FI model tailored for the DCSZ task should be elaborately designed. Compared to optical-flow-based ( Li et al. 2023 ; Cheng and Chen 2021 ; Kong et al. 2022 ; Huang et al. 2022 ; Jin et al. 2023 ) interpolation manners, diffusion-based ones ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Feng et al. 2024 ; Wan et al. 2025 ) are more suited for such large cross-view transitions, due to the powerful generative prior. However, naively applying them still encounters challenges in achieving high-fidelity transitions. On the one hand, the insufficient utilization of dual-camera images as conditional guidance in the diffusion process leads to obvious spatial artifacts and color shift in the synthesized intermediate frames. On the other hand, note that the VAE encoding process ( Rombach et al. 2022 ) inevitably incurs high-frequency information loss. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , images reconstructed from the VAE latent space contain less fine-grained details compared to the original ones. Thus, only utilizing dual images in the latent space is insufficient to achieve high-fidelity zooming. In this work, we propose ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion model for achieving smooth zoom between dual cameras, where the dual-camera images are fully employed in both latent and image spaces to address the aforementioned limitations. On the one hand, in the latent space, the dual-camera latents are directly concatenated with the input noise on the endpoints and fed into the denoising network, while their semantic features are incorporated via cross-attention mechanisms. Additionally, to prevent error accumulation between the predicted dual-camera latents and the original ones during multi-step denoising, we explicitly replace the predicted dual-camera latents with the original ones at each denoising step. On the other hand, in the image space, we note that the multi-scale feature maps extracted by the VAE encoder preserve more high-frequency details, and their appropriate utilization is important for improving fidelity. As the VAE encoding features of intermediate frames are unavailable, we first employ a pre-trained optical flow estimation network (e.g., SEA-RAFT ( Wang et al. 2024c ) ) to estimate the motion between dual-camera images and the intermediate frames. Then we warp the dual-image features to obtain features for the intermediate frames, which are injected into the VAE decoder via a ref injector module for better generation. Besides, flow-guided temporal consistency supervision is adopted to produce more smooth transitions. We conduct extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our ZoomDiff achieves photo-realistic smooth zooming between dual cameras, outperforming state-of-the-art methods both quantitatively and qualitatively. The contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion model for achieving smooth zoom transitions between dual cameras. • We suggest injecting the dual-camera images in both latent and image spaces, where latent information from the dual images is used in multiple ways to guide the denoising process for geometric consistency, while flow-aligned multi-scale features from the VAE encoder are injected into the VAE decoder to preserve high-frequency details. • Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ZoomDiff, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

sections.heading: Dual-Camera Smooth Zoom
sections.text: They proposed a data construction pipeline based on 3DGS ( Kerbl et al. 2023 ) that generates synthetic zooming sequences between dual cameras to fine-tune video frame interpolation (VFI) models ( Li et al. 2023 ; Jin et al. 2023 ; Huang et al. 2022 ; Kong et al. 2022 ) for smooth transitions. However, even with data-driven adaptation, the synthesized results often exhibit boundary artifacts and structural inconsistencies due to substantial geometric disparity in such extremely large cross-view transitions. These observations highlight the difficulty of the DCSZ task, and it is necessary to design an FI model tailored to it. sections.heading: Optical-Flow-Based Frame Interpolation
sections.text: Driven by the robustness of optical flow, flow-based manners ( Huang et al. 2022 ; Kong et al. 2022 ; Bao et al. 2019a ; Bao et al. 2019b ; Li et al. 2023 ; Jin et al. 2023 ; Liu et al. 2017 ; Niklaus and Liu 2018 ; Niklaus and Liu 2020 ; Xu et al. 2019 ; Zhang et al. 2023a ; Lu et al. 2022 ; Park et al. 2023 ) currently dominate video frame interpolation, with extensive research into novel optimization objectives ( Huang et al. 2022 ; Kong et al. 2022 ) and advanced network designs ( Bao et al. 2019a ; Bao et al. 2019b ; Li et al. 2023 ; Jin et al. 2023 ; Liu et al. 2017 ; Niklaus and Liu 2018 ; Niklaus and Liu 2020 ; Xu et al. 2019 ; Zhang et al. 2023a ; Lu et al. 2022 ; Park et al. 2023 ) . To enhance flow accuracy, existing works have proposed various strategies, ranging from task-oriented flow distillation (e.g., RIFE ( Huang et al. 2022 ) and IFRNet ( Kong et al. 2022 ) ) and advanced bidirectional correlation retrieval (e.g., AMT ( Li et al. 2023 ) and UPRNet ( Jin et al. 2023 ) ) to unified motion-appearance extraction. By relying on explicit motion modeling and geometric alignment, these methods excel at synthesizing temporally coherent frames under moderate motion. However, applying them to the DCSZ task reveals fundamental limitations. Dual-camera systems inherently introduce large cross-view disparities and progressive content occlusion. These characteristics severely violate the strict dense correspondence assumption fundamental to optical-flow estimation. Consequently, traditional flow-based models often fail to produce reliable matches, struggling to maintain sharp boundaries and detailed structures in the DCSZ task.

sections.heading: Diffusion-Based Frame Interpolation
sections.text: Recent works have extensively explored diffusion models ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Feng et al. 2024 ; Yang et al. 2024 ; Wan et al. 2025 ) for generative frame interpolation without explicitly relying on optical flow. Representative methods, such as FCVG ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) , GI ( Wang et al. 2024b ) , and TRF ( Feng et al. 2024 ) , formulate this as a conditional generation task by encoding the first and last frames as conditions for the denoising network. Furthermore, approaches such as VIBID ( Yang et al. 2024 ) , Framer ( Wang et al. 2024a ) , and the recent video foundation model Wan2.1 (FLF) ( Wan et al. 2025 ) harness the rich generative priors of large-scale diffusion models, employing advanced temporal modules to synthesize coherent intermediate dynamics. By leveraging these generative capabilities, they can hallucinate plausible structures under large appearance changes, fundamentally alleviating the strict correspondence assumptions of flow-based methods. However, naively applying existing diffusion-based FI models for the DCSZ task yields low-fidelity transitions, due to insufficient conditional guidance and high-frequency information loss during VAE encoding. In this work, we propose ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion model that utilizes dual-camera inputs in both latent and pixel spaces for photo-realistic transitions.

sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.text: Problem Formation. Dual-Camera Smooth Zoom (DCSZ) aims to achieve a fluid zoom preview between dual-cameras on a mobile phone, which can be accomplished by a frame interpolation (FI) model to synthesize F − 1 F-1 intermediate images { 𝐗 ^ i } i = 1 F − 1 \{\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{F-1} between dual-camera images 𝐗 0 \mathbf{X}_{0} and 𝐗 F \mathbf{X}_{F} . It can be written as, 𝐗 ^ i = ℱ ​ ℐ ​ ( 𝐗 0 , 𝐗 F , i , Θ ℱ ​ ℐ ) , \hat{\mathbf{{X}}}_{i}=\mathcal{FI}(\mathbf{X}_{0},\mathbf{X}_{F},i;\mathrm{\Theta_{\mathcal{FI}}}), (1) where Θ ℱ ​ ℐ \mathrm{\Theta_{\mathcal{FI}}} denotes the parameters of the FI model ℱ ​ ℐ \mathcal{FI} . i i is the temporal index that indicates the relative relationship between the i i -th synthesized image 𝐗 ^ i \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{i} and the dual-camera images. Compared to the widely explored video frame interpolation task that processes relatively smaller camera and object motion, DCSZ needs to handle the extremely large cross-view disparity and complex geometric transformations between dual cameras, making it more challenging. Diffusion Models. Generative diffusion models ( Blattmann et al. 2023 ; Chen et al. 2023 ; Wang et al. 2025 ) iteratively denoise random Gaussian noise into high-quality images or videos by a denoising network. Taking Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) ( Blattmann et al. 2023 ) , it first encodes the given video using an autoencoder to obtain the latent representation z z . The forward process gradually adds noise to z z as follows, z t = α t ​ z + σ t ​ ϵ , z_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\sigma_{t}\epsilon, (2) where ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) , α t \alpha_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} represent the noise level for denoising time t t , defined by the noise schedule. For the backward process, a denoiser is used to iteratively denoise under the image-conditioning constraint. Finally, the generated videos are obtained through the VAE decoder. Although several studies ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Feng et al. 2024 ; Yang et al. 2024 ) have endeavored to apply diffusion models to video frame interpolation, we observe that naively applying them to DCSZ still faces challenges in achieving high-fidelity transitions, due to insufficient conditional guidance for multi-step denoising and high-frequency information loss during VAE encoding. In this work, we propose ZoomDiff, a diffusion model based upon SVD ( Blattmann et al. 2023 ) for high-fidelity smooth zooming between dual cameras, as shown in Fig. 2 . Specifically, we first introduce several mechanisms to strengthen the conditional guidance of dual images during the multi-step denoising process in the latent space. Then, we explore the dual-camera images in image space by incorporating multi-scale features from the VAE encoder into the VAE decoder to preserve high-frequency details Finally, we provide the details of optimization objectives and inference acceleration. sections.heading: Utilizing Dual Images in Latent Space
sections.text: On the one hand, we encode the dual images 𝐗 0 \mathbf{X}_{0} and 𝐗 F \mathbf{X}_{F} using the pre-trained VAE encoder to obtain their latent representations 𝐙 0 \mathbf{Z}_{0} and 𝐙 F \mathbf{Z}_{F} . Then a condition sequence 𝐙 0 : F \mathbf{Z}_{0:F} is concatenated with the Gaussian noise along the channel dimension and fed into the denoising U-Net, where 𝐙 0 : F \mathbf{Z}_{0:F} can be written as, 𝐙 0 : F = [ 𝐙 0 , 0 , … , 0 , 𝐙 F ] . \mathbf{Z}_{0:F}=[\,\mathbf{Z}_{0},\;\mathbf{0},\;\ldots,\;\mathbf{0},\;\,\mathbf{Z}_{F}\,]. (3) This encourages the denoising process to follow a zoom trajectory anchored by dual images. On the other hand, we feed 𝐗 0 \mathbf{X}_{0} and 𝐗 F \mathbf{X}_{F} into a pre-trained CLIP ( Radford et al. 2021 ) encoder to extract semantic features 𝐇 0 \mathbf{H}_{0} and 𝐇 T \mathbf{H}_{T} . These features are then concatenated together and injected into the denoising U-Net via a cross-attention mechanism ( Lin et al. 2021 ) to guide the generation process, which improves global visual coherence. Additionally, we observe that errors between the predicted dual-camera latents and the original ones may accumulate during multi-step denoising, which easily leads to content and color shifts. Considering the latents of dual images 𝐙 0 \mathbf{Z}_{0} and 𝐙 F \mathbf{Z}_{F} are still available during inference, we directly replace the predicted latents of dual images 𝐙 ^ 0 t \hat{\mathbf{Z}}^{\,t}_{0} and 𝐙 ^ F t \hat{\mathbf{Z}}^{\,t}_{F} with 𝐙 0 \mathbf{Z}_{0} and 𝐙 F \mathbf{Z}_{F} respectively at each t t -th step of denoising, which can be written as, 𝐙 ^ 0 t = 𝐙 0 , 𝐙 ^ F t = 𝐙 F . \hat{\mathbf{Z}}^{\,t}_{0}=\mathbf{Z}_{0},\quad\hat{\mathbf{Z}}^{\,t}_{F}=\mathbf{Z}_{F}. (4) It explicitly anchors the latent diffusion process to dual images and stabilizes the generation of the intermediate frames.

sections.heading: Utilizing Dual Images in Image Space
sections.text: Specifically, we deploy a pre-trained optical flow network (i.e., SEA-RAFT ( Wang et al. 2024c ) ) to estimate the bidirectional optical flows (i.e., 𝐎 0 → F \mathbf{O}_{0\rightarrow F} and 𝐎 F → 0 \mathbf{O}_{F\rightarrow 0} ) between the dual images. The optical flows at i i -th intermediate timestamps (i.e., 𝐎 0 → i \mathbf{O}_{0\rightarrow i} and 𝐎 F → i \mathbf{O}_{F\rightarrow i} ) are then obtained by linear interpolation. It can be written as, O 0 → i = i F ​ O 0 → F , O F → i = ( 1 − i F ) ​ O F → 0 . O_{0\rightarrow i}=\frac{i}{F}\,O_{0\rightarrow F},\quad O_{F\rightarrow i}=(1-\frac{i}{F})\,O_{F\rightarrow 0}. (5) After that, we back warp 𝐑 0 s \mathbf{R}_{0}^{s} and 𝐑 F s \mathbf{R}_{F}^{s} with 𝐎 0 → i \mathbf{O}_{0\rightarrow i} and 𝐎 F → i \mathbf{O}_{F\rightarrow i} to obtain reference features of intermediate frames (i.e., 𝐑 0 → i s \mathbf{R}_{0\rightarrow i}^{s} and 𝐑 F → i s \mathbf{R}_{F\rightarrow i}^{s} ). It can be written as, 𝐑 0 → i s = 𝒲 ⁡ ( R 0 s , O 0 → i ) , 𝐑 F → i s = 𝒲 ⁡ ( R F s , O F → i ) , \mathbf{R}_{0\rightarrow i}^{s}=\mathcal{W}(R_{0}^{s},O_{0\rightarrow i}),\quad\mathbf{R}_{F\rightarrow i}^{s}=\mathcal{W}(R_{F}^{s},O_{F\rightarrow i}), (6) where 𝒲 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{W}(\cdot) denotes backward warping operation. Finally, 𝐑 0 → i s \mathbf{R}_{0\rightarrow i}^{s} , 𝐑 F → i s \mathbf{R}_{F\rightarrow i}^{s} and the decoder features of i i -th intermediate frame at s s -th scale 𝐃 i s \mathbf{D}_{i}^{s} are concatenated along channel dimension and then fed into a ref injector module to learn the high-frequency features, which are added with 𝐃 i s \mathbf{D}_{i}^{s} to obtain the fused feature representations 𝐃 ^ i s \mathbf{\hat{D}}_{i}^{s} . It can be written as 𝐃 ^ i s = 𝐃 i s + ℱ ⁡ ( 𝐑 0 → i s , 𝐑 F → i s , 𝐃 i s ) , \mathbf{\hat{D}}_{i}^{s}=\mathbf{D}_{i}^{s}+\mathcal{F}\big(\mathbf{R}_{0\rightarrow i}^{s},\;\mathbf{R}_{F\rightarrow i}^{s},\;\mathbf{D}_{i}^{s}\big), (7) where ℱ \mathcal{F} denotes the ref injector module. It consists of four 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolutional layers with ReLU activations followed by a 1×1 convolutional layer for channel reduction. 𝐃 ^ i s \mathbf{\hat{D}}_{i}^{s} is passed into the decoder at s − 1 s-1 scale for latter reconstruction.

sections.heading: Experimental Settings
sections.text: Datasets. We follow ( Wu et al. 2024 ) to construct 2100 sequences, including indoor and outdoor scenes, where 2000 sequences are used for training, and the non-overlapped 100 ones are used for evaluation. Each sequence comprises 14 frames at a resolution of 576 × 320 576\times 320 . Besides, we use 100 real-world scenes captured by Redmi K50 Ultra from ( Wu et al. 2024 ) to evaluate performance in the real world. Training Configurations. For stable optimization, we adopt a two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, we train the denoising U-Net for 40k iterations for coarse geometry optimization. In the second stage, the denoising U-Net is frozen, and only the parameters of the ref injector module are optimized for an additional 10k iterations for fine-grained details. The learning rate is set to 3 × 10 − 5 3\times 10^{-5} and the Adam optimizer ( Kingma and Ba 2014 ) is adopted. We augment the training data with random horizontal and vertical flips. All experiments are conducted with PyTorch ( Paszke et al. 2019 ) on two Nvidia GeForce RTX A6000 GPUs. Evaluation Configurations. During inference, we set the random seed to 42 42 for deterministic evaluation. For the synthetic dataset with ground-truth intermediate frames, we calculate full-reference metrics, including PSNR ( Huynh-Thu and Ghanbari 2008 ) , SSIM ( Wang et al. 2004 ) , and LPIPS ( Zhang et al. 2018b ) for spatial fidelity, as well as PSNR-div ( Daly et al. 2025 ) and FVD ( Unterthiner et al. 2018 ) for temporal consistency evaluation. For real-world data without ground-truth references, we employ several no-reference image and video quality assessment metrics, including MUSIQ ( Ke et al. 2021 ) , LIQE ( Zhang et al. 2023b ) , DBCNN ( Wang et al. 2023 ) , and DOVER ( Wu et al. 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
sections.text: Comparison Configurations . We compare our method with 12 state-of-the-art frame interpolation methods, including 5 optical-flow-based ones (i.e., EDSC ( Cheng and Chen 2021 ) , IFRNet ( Kong et al. 2022 ) , RIFE ( Huang et al. 2022 ) , AMT ( Li et al. 2023 ) , UPRNet ( Jin et al. 2023 ) and 6 diffusion-based ones (i.e., FCVG ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) , GI ( Wang et al. 2024b ) , TRF ( Feng et al. 2024 ) , VIBID ( Yang et al. 2024 ) , Framer ( Wang et al. 2024a ) and Wan2.1 ( Wan et al. 2025 ) ). Note that Wan2.1 ( Wan et al. 2025 ) refers to the first-last-frame-to-video version (FLF2V-14B-720P). Quantitative Results . Table 1 presents the quantitative comparison against state-of-the-art methods. On the synthetic dataset, ZoomDiff achieves the best reconstruction fidelity and temporal consistency, outperforming all competitors with PSNR of 23.80, SSIM of 0.761, LPIPS of 0.253, PSNR-div of 23.01, and FVD of 131.332. Furthermore, on the real-world dataset, ZoomDiff exhibits superior generalization capability and visual quality. It establishes new state-of-the-art performance across all no-reference image quality assessment metrics. Overall, these results validate the superiority of ZoomDiff over existing methods for generating high-fidelity, temporally consistent, and visually pleasing results in both synthetic and complex real-world scenarios. Qualitative Results . The qualitative comparisons on synthetic and real-world datasets are presented in Fig. 3 . Optical-flow-based methods ( Li et al. 2023 ; Cheng and Chen 2021 ; Kong et al. 2022 ; Huang et al. 2022 ; Jin et al. 2023 ) exhibit noticeable structural artifacts, degrading the zooming consistency. Meanwhile, diffusion-based approaches ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Wan et al. 2025 ) generate inconsistent geometry and confusing details due to inadequate dual-camera guidance and VAE-induced high-frequency loss. In contrast, by jointly exploiting the dual-camera information in both latent and image spaces, ZoomDiff produces geometrically consistent zoom transitions with photo-realistic details and fewer visual artifacts. Additional video results are provided in Suppl. .

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: We conduct ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of each component in the proposed ZoomDiff on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Specifically, we first investigate different strategies for injecting the latents of dual-image into the diffusion process. Then, we evaluate the effectiveness of injecting multi-scale image features from the VAE encoder into the VAE decoder. Finally, we study the impact of optimization objectives and few-step adaptation.

sections.heading: Effect of Dual-Image Utilization in Latent Space
sections.text: We exploit dual-image information in the latent space through three complementary designs. First, the encoded latents of the two reference images are concatenated with the noisy latents at the first and last frames, respectively. Second, their semantic features are injected into the denoising network through cross-attention to provide high-level structural guidance. Third, the predicted boundary latents are replaced with the original reference latents at each denoising step, preventing errors at the two endpoints from accumulating throughout the sequence. We validate these designs through the ablations in Table 2 . Removing the semantic features ( i.e . , w/o Semantic) weakens structural fidelity, indicating that latent inputs alone are insufficient to preserve high-level content. Without step-wise latent replacement ( i.e . , w/o Replacement), prediction errors at the boundary frames gradually accumulate, leading to brightness deviations and temporally propagated artifacts. We also investigate a naive strategy that concatenates both reference latents with every noisy latent along the channel dimension ( i.e . , Naive Concat). This indiscriminate fusion disrupts the original denoising distribution and introduces inconsistent conditioning across frames, resulting in inferior reconstruction quality and unstable brightness. By combining semantic guidance with explicit boundary anchoring, our full model achieves the best overall performance across the synthetic and real-world datasets. sections.text: To compensate for the high-frequency information lost during VAE encoding, we inject the multi-scale features of the dual-camera images from the VAE encoder into the corresponding layers of the VAE decoder. We evaluate this design by removing the feature injection while keeping the remaining components unchanged. As shown in Fig. 4 , removing the encoder features ( i.e . , w/o Injection) leads to blurred textures, weakened fine structures, and local distortions, consistent with the information loss introduced by the VAE bottleneck in Fig. 1 . In contrast, ZoomDiff provides the decoder with complementary multi-scale information from both input images, thereby preserving spatial structures and recovering sharper and more faithful details. The consistent improvements across the quantitative metrics in Table 3 further demonstrate the importance of utilizing dual-image information in the image space. sections.heading: Effect of Few-Step Adaptation
sections.text: The iterative denoising process of diffusion models incurs substantial inference overhead. We therefore adapt the converged 25-step model to 8-step and 4-step sampling schedules without modifying the network architecture. As shown in Table 5 , the resulting models achieve 2.16 × 2.16\times and 2.92 × 2.92\times inference speedups, respectively. Table 6 demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed adaptation. Compared with directly shortening the sampling trajectory, the adapted 8-step and 4-step models consistently improve all evaluation metrics. In particular, the adapted 8-step model surpasses the original 25-step model on all synthetic metrics while maintaining comparable performance on the real-world dataset. Although the 4-step model shows a moderate quality degradation relative to the 25-step model, it remains clearly superior to the unadapted 4-step variant. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we present ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion framework tailored for the Dual-Camera Smooth Zoom (DCSZ) task, where the dual-camera images are fully utilized in both the latent and the image space to improve fidelity. Specifically, we introduce multiple ways to utilize the latent information from the dual images to guide the denoising process for geometric consistency, and inject flow-aligned multi-scale features from the VAE encoder into the VAE decoder via a ref injector module to preserve high-frequency details. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that ZoomDiff outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving photo-realistic smooth zooming transitions between dual cameras. sections.text: In addition to the quantitative ablation results reported in the main paper, we provide more qualitative comparisons to analyze the effects of different design components in ZoomDiff.

sections.heading: Effect of Dual-Image Utilization in Latent Space
sections.text: We provide qualitative comparisons of different latent-space utilization strategies in Fig. 9 . Compared with our full model, removing semantic guidance (i.e., w/o Semantic) results in less accurate structural details, demonstrating that high-level semantic information from the reference images is important for preserving scene content during denoising. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2609.28083v1 [cs.CV] 23 Sep 2026 ZoomDiff: A High-Fidelity Diffusion Model for Dual-Camera Smooth Zooming Jiayi Zhang Renlong Wu Yukang Ding Sibin Deng Wangmeng Zuo Abstract Digital zoom transitions between dual cameras often exhibit conspicuous discontinuities in geometric structure and chromatic consistency, degrading the user experience. While recent dual-camera smooth zoom (DCSZ) methods attempt to mitigate this by fine-tuning frame interpolation (FI) models on DCSZ data, they struggle with the large cross-view disparities and complex geometric transformations. Considering that the generative prior of diffusion models is suitable for addressing this problem, we explore their application to DCSZ. However, naively applying existing diffusion-based FI models still yields low-fidelity transitions due to insufficient conditional guidance, high-frequency information loss during VAE encoding, as well as inadequate temporal consistency. To address this, we propose ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion model that leverages dual-camera inputs in both latent and pixel spaces for photo-realistic transitions. Specifically, we first strengthen dual-image conditional guidance during the multi-step denoising process to improve geometric consistency. Then we inject flow-aligned multi-scale features from the VAE encoder into the VAE decoder to recover high-frequency details, where flow-guided temporal consistency supervision are introduced to produce more smooth transitions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that ZoomDiff outperforms state-of-the-art methods quantitatively and qualitatively. Images reconstructed from VAE latents contain less details than the original ones as indicated by yellows boxes. Modern phones are equipped with multiple fixed-focal-length cameras for digital zoom. Taking the dual-camera system as an example, it consists of a wide-angle (W) lens for primary imaging and an ultra-wide-angle (UW) lens for an even wider view. Due to the distinct deployment locations and internal characteristics ( Zhang et al. 2022 ; Lee et al. 2022 ; Alzayer et al. 2023 ; Abdelhamed et al. 2021 ) of the two cameras, a notable preview jump in geometric content and image color occurs when zooming between them, which significantly affects the user experience as they generally prefer a fluid preview. To explore the issue, ( Wu et al. 2024 ) first formulated that task as dual-camera smooth zoom (DCSZ), and tackled it from a data-centric perspective. They proposed a data construction pipeline based on 3DGS ( Kerbl et al. 2023 ) , which generates synthetic DCSZ data to fine-tune a frame interpolation (FI) model for smooth transitions. However, the results generally suffer from noticeable visual artifacts, which severely undermine the perceptual quality and zooming consistency. We argue that the main cause lies in the inherent model-task mismatch. Specifically, mainstream optical-flow-based ( Li et al. 2023 ; Cheng and Chen 2021 ; Kong et al. 2022 ; Huang et al. 2022 ; Jin et al. 2023 ) or diffusion-based ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Feng et al. 2024 ; Wan et al. 2025 ) FI models are designed for videos with smaller camera or object motion, which cannot adapt to the large cross-view disparity and complex geometric transformations between dual cameras. In other words, a task-specific FI model tailored for the DCSZ task should be elaborately designed. Compared to optical-flow-based ( Li et al. 2023 ; Cheng and Chen 2021 ; Kong et al. 2022 ; Huang et al. 2022 ; Jin et al. 2023 ) interpolation manners, diffusion-based ones ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Feng et al. 2024 ; Wan et al. 2025 ) are more suited for such large cross-view transitions, due to the powerful generative prior. However, naively applying them still encounters challenges in achieving high-fidelity transitions. On the one hand, the insufficient utilization of dual-camera images as conditional guidance in the diffusion process leads to obvious spatial artifacts and color shift in the synthesized intermediate frames. On the other hand, note that the VAE encoding process ( Rombach et al. 2022 ) inevitably incurs high-frequency information loss. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , images reconstructed from the VAE latent space contain less fine-grained details compared to the original ones. Thus, only utilizing dual images in the latent space is insufficient to achieve high-fidelity zooming. In this work, we propose ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion model for achieving smooth zoom between dual cameras, where the dual-camera images are fully employed in both latent and image spaces to address the aforementioned limitations. On the one hand, in the latent space, the dual-camera latents are directly concatenated with the input noise on the endpoints and fed into the denoising network, while their semantic features are incorporated via cross-attention mechanisms. Additionally, to prevent error accumulation between the predicted dual-camera latents and the original ones during multi-step denoising, we explicitly replace the predicted dual-camera latents with the original ones at each denoising step. On the other hand, in the image space, we note that the multi-scale feature maps extracted by the VAE encoder preserve more high-frequency details, and their appropriate utilization is important for improving fidelity. As the VAE encoding features of intermediate frames are unavailable, we first employ a pre-trained optical flow estimation network (e.g., SEA-RAFT ( Wang et al. 2024c ) ) to estimate the motion between dual-camera images and the intermediate frames. Then we warp the dual-image features to obtain features for the intermediate frames, which are injected into the VAE decoder via a ref injector module for better generation. Besides, flow-guided temporal consistency supervision is adopted to produce more smooth transitions. We conduct extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our ZoomDiff achieves photo-realistic smooth zooming between dual cameras, outperforming state-of-the-art methods both quantitatively and qualitatively. The contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion model for achieving smooth zoom transitions between dual cameras. • We suggest injecting the dual-camera images in both latent and image spaces, where latent information from the dual images is used in multiple ways to guide the denoising process for geometric consistency, while flow-aligned multi-scale features from the VAE encoder are injected into the VAE decoder to preserve high-frequency details. • Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ZoomDiff, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Related Work Dual-Camera Smooth Zoom They proposed a data construction pipeline based on 3DGS ( Kerbl et al. 2023 ) that generates synthetic zooming sequences between dual cameras to fine-tune video frame interpolation (VFI) models ( Li et al. 2023 ; Jin et al. 2023 ; Huang et al. 2022 ; Kong et al. 2022 ) for smooth transitions. However, even with data-driven adaptation, the synthesized results often exhibit boundary artifacts and structural inconsistencies due to substantial geometric disparity in such extremely large cross-view transitions. These observations highlight the difficulty of the DCSZ task, and it is necessary to design an FI model tailored to it. To avoid the high-frequency loss during VAE encoding, image features ( i.e . , 𝐑 0 s \mathbf{R}_{0}^{s} and 𝐑 F s \mathbf{R}_{F}^{s} ) from the VAE encoder at s s -th scale are injected into the VAE decoder. Additionally, ZoomDiff is optimized by loss terms in both latent and pixel spaces. Optical-Flow-Based Frame Interpolation Driven by the robustness of optical flow, flow-based manners ( Huang et al. 2022 ; Kong et al. 2022 ; Bao et al. 2019a ; Bao et al. 2019b ; Li et al. 2023 ; Jin et al. 2023 ; Liu et al. 2017 ; Niklaus and Liu 2018 ; Niklaus and Liu 2020 ; Xu et al. 2019 ; Zhang et al. 2023a ; Lu et al. 2022 ; Park et al. 2023 ) currently dominate video frame interpolation, with extensive research into novel optimization objectives ( Huang et al. 2022 ; Kong et al. 2022 ) and advanced network designs ( Bao et al. 2019a ; Bao et al. 2019b ; Li et al. 2023 ; Jin et al. 2023 ; Liu et al. 2017 ; Niklaus and Liu 2018 ; Niklaus and Liu 2020 ; Xu et al. 2019 ; Zhang et al. 2023a ; Lu et al. 2022 ; Park et al. 2023 ) . To enhance flow accuracy, existing works have proposed various strategies, ranging from task-oriented flow distillation (e.g., RIFE ( Huang et al. 2022 ) and IFRNet ( Kong et al. 2022 ) ) and advanced bidirectional correlation retrieval (e.g., AMT ( Li et al. 2023 ) and UPRNet ( Jin et al. 2023 ) ) to unified motion-appearance extraction. By relying on explicit motion modeling and geometric alignment, these methods excel at synthesizing temporally coherent frames under moderate motion. However, applying them to the DCSZ task reveals fundamental limitations. Dual-camera systems inherently introduce large cross-view disparities and progressive content occlusion. These characteristics severely violate the strict dense correspondence assumption fundamental to optical-flow estimation. Consequently, traditional flow-based models often fail to produce reliable matches, struggling to maintain sharp boundaries and detailed structures in the DCSZ task. Diffusion-Based Frame Interpolation Recent works have extensively explored diffusion models ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Feng et al. 2024 ; Yang et al. 2024 ; Wan et al. 2025 ) for generative frame interpolation without explicitly relying on optical flow. Representative methods, such as FCVG ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) , GI ( Wang et al. 2024b ) , and TRF ( Feng et al. 2024 ) , formulate this as a conditional generation task by encoding the first and last frames as conditions for the denoising network. Furthermore, approaches such as VIBID ( Yang et al. 2024 ) , Framer ( Wang et al. 2024a ) , and the recent video foundation model Wan2.1 (FLF) ( Wan et al. 2025 ) harness the rich generative priors of large-scale diffusion models, employing advanced temporal modules to synthesize coherent intermediate dynamics. By leveraging these generative capabilities, they can hallucinate plausible structures under large appearance changes, fundamentally alleviating the strict correspondence assumptions of flow-based methods. However, naively applying existing diffusion-based FI models for the DCSZ task yields low-fidelity transitions, due to insufficient conditional guidance and high-frequency information loss during VAE encoding. In this work, we propose ZoomDiff, a high-fidelity diffusion model that utilizes dual-camera inputs in both latent and pixel spaces for photo-realistic transitions. Methods Preliminaries Problem Formation. Dual-Camera Smooth Zoom (DCSZ) aims to achieve a fluid zoom preview between dual-cameras on a mobile phone, which can be accomplished by a frame interpolation (FI) model to synthesize F − 1 F-1 intermediate images { 𝐗 ^ i } i = 1 F − 1 \{\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{F-1} between dual-camera images 𝐗 0 \mathbf{X}_{0} and 𝐗 F \mathbf{X}_{F} . It can be written as, 𝐗 ^ i = ℱ ​ ℐ ​ ( 𝐗 0 , 𝐗 F , i , Θ ℱ ​ ℐ ) , \hat{\mathbf{{X}}}_{i}=\mathcal{FI}(\mathbf{X}_{0},\mathbf{X}_{F},i;\mathrm{\Theta_{\mathcal{FI}}}), (1) where Θ ℱ ​ ℐ \mathrm{\Theta_{\mathcal{FI}}} denotes the parameters of the FI model ℱ ​ ℐ \mathcal{FI} . i i is the temporal index that indicates the relative relationship between the i i -th synthesized image 𝐗 ^ i \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{i} and the dual-camera images. Compared to the widely explored video frame interpolation task that processes relatively smaller camera and object motion, DCSZ needs to handle the extremely large cross-view disparity and complex geometric transformations between dual cameras, making it more challenging. Diffusion Models. Generative diffusion models ( Blattmann et al. 2023 ; Chen et al. 2023 ; Wang et al. 2025 ) iteratively denoise random Gaussian noise into high-quality images or videos by a denoising network. Taking Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) ( Blattmann et al. 2023 ) , it first encodes the given video using an autoencoder to obtain the latent representation z z . The forward process gradually adds noise to z z as follows, z t = α t ​ z + σ t ​ ϵ , z_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\sigma_{t}\epsilon, (2) where ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) , α t \alpha_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} represent the noise level for denoising time t t , defined by the noise schedule. For the backward process, a denoiser is used to iteratively denoise under the image-conditioning constraint. Finally, the generated videos are obtained through the VAE decoder. Although several studies ( Zhu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2024a ; Wang et al. 2024b ; Feng et al. 2024 ; Yang et al. 2024 ) have endeavored to apply diffusion models to video frame interpolation, we observe that naively applying them to DCSZ still faces challenges in achieving high-fidelity transitions, due to insufficient conditional guidance for multi-step denoising and high-frequency information loss during VAE encoding. In this work, we propose ZoomDiff, a diffusion model based upon SVD ( Blattmann et al. 2023 ) for high-fidelity smooth zooming between dual cameras, as shown in Fig. 2 . Specifically, we first introduce several mechanisms to strengthen the conditional guidance of dual images during the multi-step denoising process in the latent space. Then, we explore the dual-camera images in image space by incorporating multi-scale features from the VAE encoder into the VAE decoder to preserve high-frequency details Finally, we provide the details of optimization objectives and inference acceleration. Experiments Experimental Settings Datasets. We follow ( Wu et al. 2024 ) to construct 2100 sequences, including indoor and outdoor scenes, where 2000 sequences are used for training, and the non-overlapped 100 ones are used for evaluation. Each sequence comprises 14 frames at a resolution of 576 × 320 576\times 320 . Besides, we use 100 real-world scenes captured by Redmi K50 Ultra from ( Wu et al. 2024 ) to evaluate performance in the real world. Training Configurations. For stable optimization, we adopt a two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, we train the denoising U-Net for 40k iterations for coarse geometry optimization. In the second stage, the denoising U-Net is frozen, and only the parameters of the ref injector module are optimized for an additional 10k iterations for fine-grained details. The learning rate is set to 3 × 10 − 5 3\times 10^{-5} and the Adam optimizer ( Kingma and Ba 2014 ) is adopted. We augment the training data with random horizontal and vertical flips. All experiments are conducted with PyTorch ( Paszke et al. 2019 ) on two Nvidia GeForce RTX A6000 GPUs. Evaluation Configurations. During inference, we set the random seed to 42 42 for deterministic evaluation. For the synthetic dataset with ground-truth intermediate frames, we calculate full-reference metrics, including PSNR ( Huynh-Thu and Ghanbari 2008 ) , SSIM ( Wang et al. 2004 ) , and LPIPS ( Zhang et al. 2018b ) for spatial fidelity, as well as PSNR-div ( Daly et al. 2025 ) and FVD ( Unterthiner et al. 2018 ) for temporal consistency evaluation. For real-world data without ground-truth references, we employ several no-reference image and video quality assessment metrics, including MUSIQ ( Ke et al. 2021 ) , LIQE ( Zhang et al. 2023b ) , DBCNN ( Wang et al. 2023 ) , and DOVER ( Wu et al. 2023 ) . Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods Comparison Configurations . We compare our method with 12 state-of-the-art frame interpolation methods, including 5 optical-flow-based ones (i.e., EDSC ( Cheng and Chen 2021 ) , IFRNet ( Kong et al. 2022 ) , RIFE ( Huang et al. 2022 ) , AMT ( Li et al. 2023 ) , UPRNet ( Jin et al. 2023 ) and 6 diffusion-based ones (i.e., FCVG ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) , GI ( Wang et al. 2024b ) , TRF ( Feng et al. 2024 ) , VIBID ( Yang et al. 2024 ) , Framer ( Wang et al. 2024a ) and Wan2.1 ( Wan et al. 2025 ) ). Note that Wan2.1 ( Wan et al. 2025 ) refers to the first-last-frame-to-video version (FLF2V-14B-720P). Quantitative Results . Table 1 presents the quantitative comparison against state-of-the-art methods. On the synthetic dataset, ZoomDiff achieves the best reconstruction fidelity and temporal consistency, outperforming all competitors with PSNR of 23.80, SSIM of 0.761, LPIPS of 0.253, PSNR-div of 23.01, and FVD of 131.332. Ablation Study We conduct ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of each component in the proposed ZoomDiff on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Specifically, we first investigate different strategies for injecting the latents of dual-image into the diffusion process. Then, we evaluate the effectiveness of injecting multi-scale image features from the VAE encoder into the VAE decoder. Finally, we study the impact of optimization objectives and few-step adaptation. Effect of Dual-Image Utilization in Latent Space We exploit dual-image information in the latent space through three complementary designs. First, the encoded latents of the two reference images are concatenated with the noisy latents at the first and last frames, respectively. Second, their semantic features are injected into the denoising network through cross-attention to provide high-level structural guidance. Third, the predicted boundary latents are replaced with the original reference latents at each denoising step, preventing errors at the two endpoints from accumulating throughout the sequence. We validate these designs through the ablations in Table 2 . Removing the semantic features ( i.e . , w/o Semantic) weakens structural fidelity, indicating that latent inputs alone are insufficient to preserve high-level content. Without step-wise latent replacement ( i.e . , w/o Replacement), prediction errors at the boundary frames gradually accumulate, leading to brightness deviations and temporally propagated artifacts. We also investigate a naive strategy that concatenates both reference latents with every noisy latent along the channel dimension ( i.e . , Naive Concat). This indiscriminate fusion disrupts the original denoising distribution and introduces inconsistent conditioning across frames, resulting in inferior reconstruction quality and unstable brightness. By combining semantic guidance with explicit boundary anchoring, our full model achieves the best overall performance across the synthetic and real-world datasets. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that ZoomDiff outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving photo-realistic smooth zooming transitions between dual cameras.
